meta.title: Portuguese — Sounds and spelling
meta.subtitle: 26 letters, nasal vowels, stress and written accents — start here, beside CAPLE A1
meta.desc: How European Portuguese is read, before or beside the first word: 26 notes, one card each — the endings a beginner reads wrongly first (final -a, -e and -o are not the full vowels), ou and ei, the nasal vowels and diphthongs (ã, ão, ãe, and m or n at the end of a syllable), 15 consonant letters and pairs of letters whose sound is not the English one (c, ç, ch, g, h, j, lh, nh, qu, r, rr, s, ss, x, z), and 6 rules: where the stress falls, when it is written, the acute, the circumflex and the grave accent, and falamos against falámos. The front shows the letters. The back gives, for each position the letters can stand in, the sound in the International Phonetic Alphabet and, where the source has one, the English sound it resembles, then up to three words of the CAPLE A1 deck with a speaker beside each, the letters picked out, and the word's own transcription as it is said in Portugal. Say the word, then press the speaker and compare. Of CAPLE A1's 534 words, 296 contain one of these spellings and 51 carry a written accent. THE ORDER is the vowels and nasals, the consonants in alphabetical order, then the rules. At the app's default of ten new cards a day the deck takes 3 days; it is meant to be studied before or beside CAPLE A1. THIS IS THE PRONUNCIATION OF PORTUGAL: s and z at the end of a syllable are the sh of sheep, and an unstressed e is all but swallowed, which is why spoken European Portuguese sounds unlike its spelling and unlike Brazilian. — WHAT IS NOT HERE: no description is written for this deck. Each English comparison is a cell of the first page named below (its European half where it gives two), each sound, context and rule a cell, a note or a sentence of the second, with a cut marked […]. A row is carded only where a CAPLE A1 headword shows it, so õe (nações) and gu have no row, and the letters that sound as an English speaker expects (b, d, f, l, m, n, p, t, v) have none. The transcriptions are the English Wiktionary's, for 459 of the deck's words; a word it does not transcribe for Portugal shows none. The speaker is your device's Portuguese (Portugal) voice reading the example word, so a device that has only a Brazilian voice, or none, will not sound as the transcription reads. — English comparisons: Wikipedia, “Help:IPA/Portuguese”, revision 1385653387, read 2026-11-16. Sounds, contexts and rules: Wikipedia, “Portuguese orthography”, revision 1378741311, read 2026-11-16 (both CC BY-SA 4.0). Transcriptions: English Wiktionary, via kaikki.org (CC BY-SA 4.0). Example words and meanings: the CAPLE A1 deck on this shelf (English Wiktionary via kaikki.org, CC BY-SA 4.0).

fields.Name: the syllable before the last
fields.Says: Most multisyllabic words are stressed on the penult. […] The endings -a(s), -e(s), -o(s), -am, -em, -ens are unstressed. The stressed vowel of words with such endings is assumed to be the first one before the ending itself: bonita, bonitas, gente […].
fields.Examples:
as in
a casa/ˈka.zɐ/house
o livro/ˈli.vɾu/book
a cidade/siˈda.dɨ/city

fields.Name: the last syllable
fields.Says: Words with other endings are regarded as oxytone by default: viver, jardim, vivi, bambu […]. They require an accent when they are stressed on a syllable other than their last: táxi, fácil […].
fields.Examples:

falar/fɐˈlaɾ/to speak
o hotel/ɔˈtɛl/hotel
o jardim/ʒɐɾˈdĩ/garden
o táxi/ˈtak.si/taxi (vehicle)
fácil/ˈfa.sil/easy (requiring little skill or effort)

fields.Name: an accent where the stress is not the expected one
fields.Says: All words stressed on the antepenult take an accent mark. […] If the word happens to be stressed elsewhere, it requires an accent mark: será, serás, até […].

a música/ˈmu.zi.kɐ/music (melodic and rhythmic sounds made as art)

fields.Letters: á é ó · â ê ô
fields.Name: the acute and the circumflex
fields.Says: The acute accent (◌́) and the circumflex accent (◌̂) indicate that a vowel is stressed and the quality of the accented vowel and, more precisely, its height: á, é, and ó are low vowels (except in nasal vowels); â, ê, and ô are high vowels. They also distinguish a few homographs: por "by" with pôr "to put" […].

fields.Name: the grave accent
fields.Says: The grave accent (◌̀) marks the contraction of two consecutive vowels in adjacent words (crasis), normally the preposition a and an article or a demonstrative pronoun: a + aquela = àquela "at that", a + a = à "at the". It can also be used when indicating time: "às 4 horas" = "at 4 o'clock". It does not indicate stress.

as in
a/ɐ/to (introduces the indirect object)

fields.Name: we speak, we spoke
fields.Says: In European Portuguese, a distinction is made in the first person plural of verbs in -ar, between the present tense ending -amos /ˈɐmuʃ/ and the preterite -ámos /ˈamuʃ/. As these are pronounced identically in Brazilian Portuguese, this accent is not used.
